blocks.text: **The problem.** Given a string `expression` of numbers and the operators `+`, `-` and `*`, return **all** the results you can get by adding parentheses in every possible way. The answers can be in any order, with repeats.

blocks.alt: 2*3-4*5 split at each operator. Splitting at the first * gives 2 times every result of 3-4*5, which are -17 and -5: -34 and -10. Splitting at the - gives every result of 2*3 minus every result of 4*5: 6 - 20 = -14. Splitting at the last * gives every result of 2*3-4, which are -2 and 2, times 5: -10 and 10. All together: -34, -10, -14, -10, 10.

elements.text: the last operator to run splits the expression in two: solve each side
elements.originalText: the last operator to run splits the expression in two: solve each side

blocks.text: The idea: divide and conquer at each operator

Every way of adding parentheses has a **last** operation — the one applied at the very end. If that's the operator at position `i`, the left side and the right side are independent smaller expressions, each with its own list of possible results. So: for every operator, recursively get all results of the left part and of the right part, and combine **every pair** with that operator. An expression with no operator is just a number — the base case.

blocks.caption: Each call splits its expression at every operator, solves both sides, and combines every pair of results.

blocks.text: **Time and space grow like the Catalan numbers** — the number of ways to parenthesise n operators (1, 2, 5, 14, 42, …), about 4ⁿ / n^1.5. That's also the size of the output, so no algorithm can do fundamentally better.
The same piece, like `3-4`, is solved from many different splits. Cache the result list for each substring.
**Same worst case** (the output itself is that big), but far less repeated work on longer expressions. The keys are substrings; with indices `(start, end)` as keys the cache is O(n²) entries.

rows.timeWhy: Every way to split at an operator is tried: there are **Catalan(n)** results, each built with O(n) work.
rows.spaceWhy: The lists of results **themselves** are that big.

rows.timeWhy: The output is still that big, but each sub-expression is **solved only once**.
rows.spaceWhy: The memo holds the results of each sub-expression.

items: **Multi-digit numbers** — parse the whole run of digits, not one character.
**Repeated results** — `"2*3-4*5"` returns -10 twice; both are kept.
**Unique Binary Search Trees II** — the same split: every root, every left tree × every right tree.
**Burst Balloons** — choose the **last** balloon to burst in a range: divide and conquer with memoization (Dynamic Programming course).
**Expression Add Operators** — insert operators between digits to hit a target: backtracking.
